name: Daniel
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew and Aramaic Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition). Daniel is one of two bilingual books of the Old Testament: 1:1–2:4a and 8:1–12:13 are in Hebrew, while 2:4b–7:28 is in Aramaic. Both the Old Greek (Septuagint) translation of Daniel and the later Greek version attributed to Theodotion have been consulted. The Old Greek differs considerably from the Masoretic Text, especially in chapters 4–6; the early church replaced it with Theodotion, which is much closer to the Hebrew-Aramaic text, and the Old Greek survives in only a few manuscripts. Eight manuscripts of Daniel were found at Qumran (1QDan-a, 1QDan-b, 4QDan-a through 4QDan-e, and 6QDan), some copied within a few generations of the book’s completion; as reported in the published editions they generally support the Masoretic Text, preserve the changes between Hebrew and Aramaic at the same points, and contain none of the Greek additions. Daniel also has Greek additions: Azariah’s prayer and the hymn of the three young men (inserted after 3:23), the story of Susanna, and the story of Bel and the Dragon. These are not part of the Hebrew-Aramaic text and will be translated with the Apocrypha. Verse numbers follow the standard English numbering: English 4:1–3 is 3:31–33 in the Aramaic text (so English 4:4–37 is Aramaic 4:1–34), and English 5:31 is Aramaic 6:1 (so English 6:1–28 is Aramaic 6:2–29). Significant variants and difficult readings are footnoted.

verses.text: In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah,{a} Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and laid siege to it.

And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, together with part of the vessels of God’s house. These he brought to the land of Shinar,{b} to the house of his god, placing the vessels in his god’s treasure house.
Then the king told Ashpenaz, the chief of his court officials,{c} to bring some of the Israelites, both of the royal family and of the nobility—

young men without any defect, good-looking, skilled in every kind of wisdom, well informed, quick to understand, and able to serve in the king’s palace—and to teach them the literature and language of the Chaldeans.{d}
The king allotted them a daily portion of the royal food and of his own wine. Their education was to last three years, after which they would stand before the king.
Among them, from the people of Judah, were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.{e}
The chief official gave them new names: to Daniel he gave the name Belteshazzar, to Hananiah Shadrach, to Mishael Meshach, and to Azariah Abednego.{f}
But Daniel made up his mind not to defile himself with the royal food or with the king’s wine, and he sought leave from the chief official not to defile himself.
God had caused the chief official to show Daniel favor and compassion,

and the chief official told Daniel, “I fear my lord the king, who has appointed what you eat and drink. If he sees your faces thinner than those of the youths of your own age, why should that be? You would put my head in danger with the king.”
Then Daniel spoke to the steward{g} whom the chief official had put in charge of Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:
“Test your servants, I beg you, for ten days. Have them give us vegetables to eat and water to drink.
Then look at our faces and at the faces of the youths who eat the royal food, and treat your servants as you find.”
So he consented to them in this matter and proved them for ten days.
When the ten days were over, their faces looked better and they were fuller in flesh than any of the youths who ate the royal food.
From then on the steward kept taking away their food and the wine meant for them to drink and gave them vegetables.
To these four young men God gave knowledge and skill in all literature and wisdom, and Daniel could understand visions and dreams of every kind.
At the end of the time the king had set for them to be brought in, the chief official brought them before Nebuchadnezzar.
The king talked with them, and among them all no one was found equal to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. So they entered the king’s service.
In every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king asked them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his whole kingdom.
Daniel continued there until the first year of King Cyrus.{h}

notes.text: That is, 605 BC. Jeremiah 25:1 and 46:2 date Nebuchadnezzar’s first year to Jehoiakim’s fourth year; the difference probably reflects different ways of counting a king’s first year (Babylonian versus Judean reckoning).
An ancient name for Babylonia (compare Genesis 10:10; 11:2).
Hebrew saris, often “eunuch,” but also used of high court officials in general; likewise in verses 7–11 and 18.
In Daniel “Chaldeans” usually means a class of learned men skilled in astrology and divination, as well as the people of Babylonia.
The Hebrew names mean: Daniel, “God is my judge”; Hananiah, “Yahweh has been gracious”; Mishael, probably “Who is what God is?”; Azariah, “Yahweh has helped.”

The new names are Babylonian. Belteshazzar probably represents Akkadian Balaṭ-šarri-uṣur, “protect the king’s life” (Daniel 4:8 connects it with the god Bel). Shadrach and Meshach are of uncertain meaning. Abednego probably means “servant of Nego,” perhaps a deliberate alteration of Nabu, the Babylonian god of wisdom. In the Aramaic chapters the king and others usually call Daniel by his Babylonian name.
Hebrew melzar, probably a title (“guardian, steward”) rather than a personal name; the KJV took it as a name, “Melzar.”
539 BC, when Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. Daniel 10:1 records a vision in Cyrus’s third year.

verses.text: In the second year of his reign,{a} Nebuchadnezzar had dreams; his spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him.
So the king gave orders to summon the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans to tell the king his dreams. They came in and stood before the king.
The king said to them, “I have had a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know what the dream was.”
Then the Chaldeans spoke to the king in Aramaic:{b} “O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will give its interpretation.”
The king replied to the Chaldeans, “The matter is settled on my part:{c} unless you make known to me both the dream and what it means, you will be cut to pieces and your houses made a dunghill.
But if you tell me the dream and its interpretation, you will receive from me gifts and rewards and great honor. So tell me the dream and its interpretation.”
They answered a second time, “Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will give its interpretation.”
The king answered, “I know for certain that you are trying to gain time, because you see that my decision is firm:

Unless you make the dream known to me, there is just one law for you. You have plotted to speak lying and corrupt words before me until the times change. So tell me the dream, and I will know that you can show me its interpretation.”
The Chaldeans replied before the king, “No one on earth can show what the king demands! No king, however great and mighty, has asked anything like this of any magician, enchanter, or Chaldean.
What the king asks is too difficult, and there is no one who can reveal it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortals.”
At this the king became furious and very angry and ordered all the wise men of Babylon to be destroyed.
The order was issued that the wise men be executed, and officers searched for Daniel and his friends so they could be executed too.
Daniel responded with tact and good judgment to Arioch, commander of the royal guard, who had set out to execute Babylon’s wise men.
He said to Arioch, the king’s captain, “Why is the king’s decree so urgent?” And Arioch told Daniel the matter.
Daniel went in and requested of the king that he would grant him time to show the king the interpretation.
Then Daniel went to his house and told the matter to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions,
and urged them to ask for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his companions would not be destroyed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.
Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night, and Daniel blessed the God of heaven.

Daniel spoke and said:
“Blessed be the name of God
forever and ever,
for wisdom and might are his.

God of my ancestors,
I thank you and praise you,
because you gave me wisdom and strength,
and now you have shown me what we begged of you;
you have revealed to us the king’s concern.”

Daniel then went in to Arioch, the man the king had appointed to execute Babylon’s wise men. He said to him, “The wise men of Babylon must not be killed. Bring me before the king, and the meaning of his dream is what I will give him.”
Arioch hurried Daniel in before the king and told him, “I have found among the exiles of Judah a man who will make the interpretation known to the king.”
The king said to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, “Are you able to make known to me the dream I saw and its interpretation?”
Daniel replied to the king, “The mystery the king is asking about is something no wise man, sorcerer, magician or astrologer can explain to the king.

But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and he has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days. Your dream and the visions of your head as you lay on your bed were these:
As for you, O king, as you lay on your bed, your thoughts turned to what would happen after this, and the Revealer of mysteries has made known to you what is to come.

But as for me, this mystery was not revealed to me because of any wisdom in me greater than that of all living, but in order that the king might be told the interpretation, and that you might know the thoughts of your heart.
“You were watching, O king, and there before you was a great statue. That statue was huge and its brilliance extraordinary; it stood in front of you, and its appearance was terrifying.
The head of this statue was of fine gold, its chest and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze,
its legs were iron, and its feet part iron and part clay.{d}
You kept watching until a stone was cut out without hands. It struck the image on its iron and clay feet and broke them in pieces.

At that moment the iron, clay, bronze, silver and gold were broken to pieces together and became like the chaff on a summer threshing floor. The wind carried them off, leaving no trace of them. But the rock that hit the statue grew into an immense mountain and covered the entire earth.
“Such was the dream; its interpretation we will now tell before the king.
You, O king, are the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, the might, and the glory.
Wherever people live, he has given into your hand the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky, and has made you ruler over them all. You are that head of gold.
After you another kingdom will arise, inferior to yours, and then a third kingdom, of bronze, which will rule over the whole earth.
After that, a fourth kingdom will arise, as hard as iron; iron crushes and breaks everything, and like iron that smashes, this kingdom will crush and break all the others.{e}
And as you saw the feet and the toes, part potter’s clay and part iron, it will be a divided kingdom; yet some of the iron’s firmness will be in it, since you saw iron mixed with miry clay.
As the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so the kingdom will be partly strong and partly brittle.
And as you saw the iron mixed with miry clay, they will mingle with one another by marriage,{f} but they will not cling together, even as iron does not mix with clay.

In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed; its rule will not pass to another people. It will break in pieces and make an end of all these kingdoms, but it will itself stand forever—

It is as you saw: a rock was chiseled from a mountain, though no human hand was involved, and it pulverized the iron, bronze, clay, silver and gold. The great God is informing the king about what will occur afterward. The dream is true, and its interpretation can be trusted.”
Then King Nebuchadnezzar bowed down with his face to the ground and honored Daniel, and he gave orders to present a grain offering and incense to him.
The king answered Daniel, “Truly your God is God of gods and Lord of kings and the revealer of mysteries, since you could reveal this mystery.”
The king then gave Daniel a high position and many generous gifts. He made him governor of the entire province of Babylon and head over all of Babylon’s wise men.
Daniel asked the king to appoint Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon, and the king did so; Daniel himself remained at the king’s court.{g}

notes.text: About 603 BC. This seems to fall within the three years of training in 1:5; by inclusive reckoning, part-years may have been counted as whole years, and 1:18–20 need not come after 2:1 in time.

Hebrew ʾaramit, “in Aramaic.” From here through 7:28 the book is written in Aramaic, the common language of the Babylonian and Persian empires; at 8:1 it returns to Hebrew. The word “in Aramaic” may originally have been a scribal notice marking the change of language. The Qumran fragments that cover these passages show the same switches of language. Why the book is bilingual is debated; the Aramaic section (2:4b–7:28) is arranged as a unit, with chapters 2 and 7 (four kingdoms), 3 and 6 (deliverance from death), and 4 and 5 (the humbling of kings) matching each other.
Or “The word has gone out from me.” The Aramaic azda is a Persian loanword, “certain, publicly known.”
Aramaic khasaf, baked clay or earthenware, as in potters’ ware (verse 41); likewise in verses 34–35 and 41–45.

The identity of the four kingdoms is much discussed. The traditional Jewish and Christian view is Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece, and Rome; many modern scholars hold Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece (Alexander and his successors), which fits the later visions (compare 5:28, 31; 8:20–21). Compare chapter 7.
Aramaic “by the seed of men,” probably referring to marriage alliances between ruling houses (compare 11:6, 17).
Aramaic “in the gate of the king,” the place of royal administration.

verses.text: King Nebuchadnezzar made a statue of gold, about 90 feet high and 9 feet wide,{a} and set it up on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.

Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent to gather the satraps, prefects, governors, counselors, treasurers, judges, magistrates, and every official of the provinces, that they should come to the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.{b}

Then the satraps, prefects, governors, counselors, treasurers, judges, magistrates, and every official of the provinces gathered to the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up, and they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
Then the herald called out loudly, “People of every nation and language, you are commanded:
that whenever you hear the sound of horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe,{c} and all kinds of music, you shall fall down and worship the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.
Whoever does not fall down and worship shall in that same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace.”

So as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, and every kind of music, all the people of every nation and language fell down and worshiped the statue of gold that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
At that time certain Chaldeans came near and maliciously accused the Jews.{d}
They said to King Nebuchadnezzar, “O king, live forever!
You, O king, have made a decree that every man who hears the sound of horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and all kinds of music shall fall down and worship the golden image,
and whoever does not fall down and worship shall be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace.

There are certain Jews whom you appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These men, O king, have not regarded you; your gods they do not serve, and the golden image you set up they do not worship.”
Then Nebuchadnezzar, in a furious rage, ordered Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to be brought in. So these men were brought before the king.
Nebuchadnezzar spoke to them: “Is it on purpose, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods nor worship the golden image I have set up?

Now, if you are prepared, then when you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes and every other instrument, you must bow down and worship the statue I made; that will be fine. But if you refuse to worship, you will be thrown at once into the blazing furnace. And what god can rescue you from my power?”
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered the king, “Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to give you an answer on this matter.
If it is so,{e} our God whom we serve is able to rescue us from the blazing fiery furnace, and he will rescue us from your hand, O king.
But even if he does not, you should know, Your Majesty, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you set up.”
Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with rage, and his face was distorted with anger at Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He gave orders to heat the furnace seven times hotter than it was usually heated,
and he ordered some of the strongest men in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and throw them into the blazing fiery furnace.
So these men were bound in their cloaks, their trousers, their caps, and their other garments,{f} and were thrown into the blazing fiery furnace.
The king’s command was so strict and the furnace so extremely hot that the flames killed the men who lifted up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.
And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell bound into the middle of the blazing fiery furnace.{g}
Then King Nebuchadnezzar leaped to his feet in astonishment. “Weren’t there three men that we bound and threw into the fire?” he asked his counselors. “Certainly, Your Majesty,” they answered.
He said, “Look, I see four men walking around loose in the fire, and they are not hurt at all; and the fourth looks like a son of the gods.”{h}

Nebuchadnezzar approached the door of the blazing furnace and called, “Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, you servants of the Most High God, come out and come here!” Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego then came out of the fire.

And the satraps, prefects, governors, and the king’s counselors gathered and saw these men, that the fire had no power over their bodies; not a hair of their heads was singed, their cloaks were unchanged, and no smell of fire had come upon them.

Nebuchadnezzar declared, “Praise to the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who sent his angel and saved his servants! They trusted in him, disobeyed the king’s order, and risked their lives rather than serve or worship any god other than their own God.

I therefore decree that any person of any people, nation or language who speaks against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego will be cut into pieces and his house reduced to a heap of ruins, since no other god can rescue people in this way.”
Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

notes.text: Aramaic “sixty cubits high and six cubits wide” (about 27 by 2.7 meters). The tall, narrow proportions suggest an image on a high pedestal or an obelisk-like monument. The Septuagint dates the event to Nebuchadnezzar’s eighteenth year (compare Jeremiah 52:29).
Several of these titles are Persian loanwords, and the exact functions of some are uncertain.
The identification of several instruments is uncertain. Three of the names (qitharos “lyre,” pesanterin “harp,” and sumponyah, perhaps “bagpipe” or “drum,” or “playing together”) are Greek loanwords.
Aramaic “ate the pieces of the Jews,” an idiom for slander or malicious accusation.
Or “If our God whom we serve is able to rescue us, he will rescue us…” The Aramaic can be read either way.
The exact meaning of these words for clothing is uncertain.

At this point the Greek versions (both the Old Greek and Theodotion) add 68 verses not found in the Hebrew-Aramaic text: the Prayer of Azariah, a short prose account of the fire and of the angel who came down into the furnace, and the Song of the Three Young Men (“Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord…”). These additions are part of Daniel in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and appear among the Apocrypha in Protestant Bibles. They will be translated in the CJT’s Apocrypha, together with the other Greek additions to Daniel, Susanna and Bel and the Dragon.

Or “a divine being.” In Aramaic “son of the gods” means a being of the divine class; verse 28 calls him God’s “angel.” The KJV’s “the Son of God” reads the phrase in the light of later Christian interpretation.

verses.text: King Nebuchadnezzar, to all peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth:{a} May your peace abound!
It has seemed good to me to make known the signs and wonders that the Most High God has done for me.

How great are his signs,
how mighty his wonders!
His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom,
and his dominion is from generation to generation.
I, Nebuchadnezzar, was living at ease in my house, flourishing in my palace.
I saw a dream that made me afraid; the imaginings on my bed and the visions of my head alarmed me.
So I issued a decree that all the wise men of Babylon should be brought in before me to make known to me the dream’s interpretation.
Then the magicians, sorcerers, Chaldeans and astrologers came in. I described the dream to them, but they could not tell me what it meant.
Finally Daniel came before me—his name is Belteshazzar, after the name of my god,{b} and he has the spirit of the holy gods in him—and I described the dream to him:

“Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that nothing puzzling is beyond you. Listen to the visions I saw in my dream, and give me the interpretation.

These were the visions in my mind as I lay in bed:
I looked, and there in the middle of the earth stood a tree,
and it was very tall.

The tree grew large and strong,
its top reached to heaven,
and it could be seen to the ends of the whole earth.

Its leaves were lovely and its fruit abundant,
and in it was food for all.
Under it the beasts of the field found shade,
in its branches the birds of the sky lived,
and from it all flesh was fed.
“In the visions of my head upon my bed I watched, and look—a watcher, a holy one,{c} descending from heaven.

He called out loudly, saying:
‘Hew the tree down and cut away its branches,
shake off its foliage and scatter its fruit.
Let the animals run from beneath it,
the birds from its boughs.

But leave the stump with its roots in the ground,
wrapped in a band of iron and bronze,
among the fresh grass of the field.
Let him be soaked with the dew of the sky,
and let him share the plants of the earth with the animals.

Let his mind be changed from a man’s,
and let the mind of a beast be given to him,
and let seven times{d} pass over him.

This sentence is announced by the watchers,
this verdict is given by the holy ones,
so that everyone alive will recognize
that the Most High is ruler over human kingdoms,
gives them to anyone he chooses,
and puts the lowest of people in charge of them.’

This is the dream I, King Nebuchadnezzar, have seen. You, Belteshazzar, declare its meaning, because all the wise men in my kingdom are unable to make the interpretation known to me; but you can, for a spirit of the holy gods is in you.”

Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was dismayed for a time, and his thoughts alarmed him. The king said, “Belteshazzar, let neither the dream nor its meaning trouble you.” Belteshazzar replied, “My lord, would that the dream were for your haters, and its meaning for your foes!
The tree that you saw grow great and strong, its top reaching to heaven, visible to all the earth,
It had beautiful leaves and plenty of fruit, with food on it for everyone; animals of the field lived in its shade, and birds of the sky nested in its branches—
it is you, O king, who have grown great and strong. Your greatness has grown and reaches to heaven, and your dominion to the end of the earth.

You saw a watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven and announcing, ‘Chop down the tree and destroy it, but leave the stump with its roots in the ground, wrapped in a band of iron and bronze, among the fresh grass of the field; let it be soaked with the dew of the sky and share the plants of the field with the animals, until seven periods of time go by for him.’
Here is the interpretation, Your Majesty: this is a decree of the Most High, and it concerns my lord the king.

People will drive you away, and you will make your home with the wild animals. You will graze on grass like cattle, with the dew of the sky soaking you. Seven periods of time will go by over you before you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of humankind and hands them to whomever he chooses.
And as it was commanded to leave the stump of the tree’s roots, your kingdom will be restored to you from the time you know that Heaven{e} rules.
Therefore, Your Majesty, please accept my advice: put an end to your sins by doing what is right, and to your wrongdoing by being kind to the poor. Then perhaps your well-being will last.”
All this came upon King Nebuchadnezzar.
Twelve months later, as he walked upon the royal palace of Babylon,
and the king said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built as a royal residence by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?”
While the words were still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: “To you it is spoken, King Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom has departed from you!

People will drive you away, and you will make your home with the wild animals. You will graze on grass like cattle. Seven periods of time will go by over you before you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of humankind and hands them to whomever he chooses.”

Right at that moment the word about Nebuchadnezzar came true. He was driven away from people and ate grass like cattle, and his body was soaked with the dew of the sky, until his hair grew as long as eagle feathers and his nails like the claws of a bird.{f}

At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, raised my eyes to heaven, and my understanding came back to me. Then I blessed the Most High; I praised and honored the one who lives forever:
For his dominion is an everlasting dominion,
and his kingdom from generation to generation.

All who dwell on the earth are reckoned as nothing,
and he does according to his will in heaven’s army
and among earth’s inhabitants;
none can stay his hand
or ask him, “What are you doing?”

At that same time my understanding came back to me, and for the glory of my kingdom my majesty and brightness returned to me. My counselors and my nobles came looking for me; I was established again in my kingdom, and surpassing greatness was added to me.
Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, offer praise, glory and honor to the King of heaven. All that he does is true, his ways are just, and he has the power to humble those who walk in arrogance.

notes.text: Verses 1–3 are 3:31–33 in the Aramaic text, and verses 4–37 are 4:1–34. The Old Greek of chapter 4 is considerably longer and differently arranged, placing this proclamation at the end of the chapter; Theodotion follows the Aramaic.
That is, Bel (Marduk), chief god of Babylon. The king connects the name with Bel by popular association (compare the note at 1:7).
Aramaic ʿir, “wakeful one,” a heavenly being who keeps watch; elsewhere in the Bible only in verses 17 and 23. The term became common in later Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch.
Probably seven years (so the Old Greek), though the word means simply “periods of time.”
This is the only place in the Old Testament where “Heaven” stands for God, a usage common in later Judaism (compare “the kingdom of heaven” in Matthew).

No Babylonian record mentions such an illness of Nebuchadnezzar. A fragmentary Aramaic text from Qumran, the Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242), as reported tells of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, being stricken for seven years in Teima and being healed when a Jewish exile urged him to honor God. Many scholars think the story in Daniel is related to such a tradition.

verses.text: King Belshazzar{a} made a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, and he drank wine in front of the thousand.

Under the influence of the wine, Belshazzar gave an order to bring the gold and silver vessels that his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem, so that the king, his nobles, his wives and his concubines could drink from them.
So they brought in the golden vessels taken from the temple, God’s house at Jerusalem, and the king drank from them, with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines.
While drinking the wine, they praised the gods made of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone.
Suddenly the fingers of a human hand appeared and began writing on the plaster of the royal palace wall, across from the lampstand; and the king watched the hand as it wrote.
Then the king’s color changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; the joints of his hips gave way, and his knees knocked against each other.

The king shouted for the sorcerers, Chaldeans and astrologers to be brought in. He told Babylon’s wise men, “Anyone who can read this inscription and explain it to me will be dressed in purple, have a gold chain placed on his neck, and be made the third highest ruler in the kingdom.”{b}
So all the king’s wise men came in, but none of them could read the inscription or explain its meaning to the king.
So King Belshazzar was greatly alarmed, his color changed, and his nobles were perplexed.
Because of what the king and his nobles had said, the queen{c} came into the banquet house. The queen spoke: “O king, live forever! Let not your thoughts alarm you, nor your color change.

There is a man in your kingdom who has the spirit of the holy gods. During your father’s reign he showed brightness, understanding and wisdom comparable to the wisdom of the gods, and your father King Nebuchadnezzar appointed him chief of the magicians, sorcerers, Chaldeans and astrologers—yes, your father the king did so—

since an excellent spirit, with knowledge and insight for interpreting dreams, explaining riddles, and solving problems,{d} was found in him—in Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar. Let Daniel be summoned now, and he will declare the interpretation.”
Then they brought Daniel in before the king, who said to him, “So you are Daniel, one of the captives from Judah that my father the king brought out of Judah?
I have heard of you, that a spirit of the gods is in you, and that light and understanding and extraordinary wisdom are found in you.
Just now the wise men, the enchanters, were brought in before me to read this writing and make known to me its interpretation, but they could not show the interpretation of the matter.

But I have heard that you can give interpretations and solve problems. Now if you can read the writing and make known to me its interpretation, you will be clothed in purple, with a chain of gold around your neck, and will rule as third in the kingdom.”
Then Daniel answered before the king, “Keep your gifts for yourself, and give your rewards to someone else. Nevertheless I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation.
Your Majesty, the Most High God gave your father Nebuchadnezzar a kingdom, greatness, glory and splendor.

Because of the greatness God gave him, people of every nation and language shook with fear in front of him. He put to death anyone he wished and spared anyone he wished; he promoted anyone he wished and demoted anyone he wished.
But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit grew hard so that he acted proudly, he was brought down from his royal throne, and his glory was taken from him.

He was expelled from human company; his mind became like an animal’s, and he lived among the wild donkeys. He grazed on grass like cattle, with the dew of the sky soaking his body, until he acknowledged that the Most High God rules over the kingdoms of humankind and puts in charge whomever he chooses.
And you, his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this.

You have set yourself up against the Lord of heaven. The vessels from his house were brought to you, and with them you, your nobles, your wives and your concubines drank your wine. You sang praises to gods of silver, gold, bronze, iron, wood and stone, which neither see nor hear nor know; but the God who holds your very breath in his hand, and owns all your paths, you did not glorify.
That is why the hand was sent out from him, and this writing was written.
“This is the writing that was inscribed: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN.{e}
Here is what the words mean: MENE—God has numbered your kingdom and finished it.
TEKEL, you have been weighed in the scales and found lacking.
PERES, your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.”
Then at Belshazzar’s command they clothed Daniel in purple, put a chain of gold around his neck, and proclaimed concerning him that he should rule as third in the kingdom.
That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed.
And Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.{f}

notes.text: Belshazzar (Babylonian Bel-šarra-uṣur, “Bel, protect the king”) was the son of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, and ruled as regent in Babylon during his father’s long absence in Arabia. Nebuchadnezzar is called his “father” (verses 2, 11, 13, 18) in the sense of predecessor, as often in ancient usage. Babylon fell to the Persians in October 539 BC.
That is, after Nabonidus and Belshazzar himself; or “as one of three rulers” (compare 6:2).
Probably the queen mother, since the king’s wives are already at the feast (verses 2–3).
Aramaic “loosen knots,” perhaps also an allusion to undoing spells; likewise in verse 16.

These words are Aramaic names of weights or monetary units: the mina (about 1¼ pounds or 570 grams), the shekel (about 0.4 ounce or 11.5 grams), and half-minas (peres, plural parsin). Daniel reads them as verbs: mene, “numbered”; tekel, “weighed”; peres, “divided,” with a further play on Paras, “Persia.” The Old Greek and Theodotion and Josephus have only three words (mene, tekel, peres).

This verse is 6:1 in the Aramaic text. Darius the Mede is not known from sources outside the Bible. He has been identified with Gubaru (Gobryas), Cyrus’s governor of Babylon, or with Cyrus himself (reading 6:28 as “Darius, that is, Cyrus the Persian”); many scholars think the book reflects a scheme in which a Median kingdom followed Babylon (compare 2:39; 7:5; 8:20).

verses.text: It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom a hundred and twenty satraps,{a} to be throughout the whole kingdom,
and over them three chief ministers, of whom Daniel was one, so that the satraps might give account to them and the king might suffer no loss.
Soon this Daniel was outperforming the other administrators and the satraps, because he had an outstanding spirit, and the king intended to appoint him over the entire kingdom.

Then the ministers and satraps tried to find a pretext against Daniel in regard to the kingdom, but they could find neither pretext nor fault, since he was trustworthy; no error or fault could be found in him.
So these men said, “We will find no pretext against this Daniel except in connection with the law of his God.”
Then these ministers and satraps came thronging{b} to the king and said to him, “King Darius, live forever!

All the ministers of the kingdom, the prefects and satraps, the counselors and governors, have agreed that the king should issue a statute and make a firm prohibition: whoever asks a petition of any god or man for thirty days, except of you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions.
Now, O king, establish the prohibition and sign the writing, that it may not be altered, by the law of the Medes and Persians, which is never repealed.”
Therefore King Darius signed the document and the interdict.

When Daniel knew that the document had been signed, he went into his house. In his upper room he had windows open toward Jerusalem, and three times a day he knelt on his knees and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done before.{c}
Then these men came thronging and found Daniel making petition and supplication before his God.

Then they approached and spoke before the king concerning the king’s prohibition: “Have you not signed a prohibition that anyone who asks a petition of any god or man within thirty days, except of you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?” The king replied, “That is certain, by the law of the Medes and Persians, which is never repealed.”
Then they said before the king, “That Daniel, one of the exiles of Judah, has no regard for you, O king, nor for the prohibition you signed; three times a day he makes his petition.”
When the king heard these words, he was much distressed, and set his mind on delivering Daniel; and until the sun went down he labored to rescue him.
Then the men rushed in to the king and told him, “Remember, Your Majesty, that under the law of the Medes and Persians no decree or edict the king issues can be altered.”
So the king commanded, and Daniel was brought and thrown into the lions’ den. The king spoke to Daniel: “Your God, whom you serve without ceasing, will deliver you!”
A stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and with the signet of his nobles, so that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.
Then the king returned to his palace and passed the night fasting; no diversions{d} were brought before him, and sleep fled from him.
Then at dawn, at first light, the king arose and went in haste to the den of lions.

When he drew near the den, he called to Daniel with a voice full of anguish. The king said, “Daniel, servant of the living God, your God whom you serve without ceasing—has he been able to deliver you from the lions?”
Then Daniel said to the king, “O king, live forever!
My God has sent his angel and closed the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me, for I was found blameless before him; and before you too, O king, I have committed no crime.”
Then the king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel up out of the den. So Daniel was lifted out of the den, and no injury of any kind was found on him, for he had trusted in his God.

Then the king gave orders, and those who had maliciously accused Daniel{e} were brought in and cast into the den of lions, together with their children and their wives. Before they reached the floor of the den, the lions seized them and crushed all their bones.
Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth: “May your peace abound!

He rescues and he delivers;
he performs signs and wonders
in the heavens and on the earth,
for he has delivered Daniel
from the paw of the lions.”
So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.{f}

notes.text: Verses 1–28 are 6:2–29 in the Aramaic text. The number of satrapies under the Persian kings varied; compare Esther 1:1 (127 provinces).
Or “came by agreement”; the Aramaic verb is used again in verses 11 and 15.
On praying toward Jerusalem compare 1 Kings 8:35, 44, 48; on three times a day compare Psalm 55:17.
The meaning of the Aramaic word is uncertain; suggestions include “musicians,” “concubines,” and “food.”
Aramaic “had eaten the pieces of Daniel”; see the note at 3:8.
Or “in the reign of Darius, that is, in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.” See the note at 5:31.

verses.text: In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon,{a} Daniel saw a dream and visions of his head as he lay on his bed. He then wrote down the dream, telling the sum of the matters.
Daniel declared: “I was looking in my vision by night, and there were the four winds of heaven stirring up the great sea.{b}
Four great beasts came up out of the sea, each different from the others.

The first was like a lion, with an eagle’s wings. I watched until its wings were plucked away; it was raised up from the earth and made to stand on two feet like a human being, and a human heart was given to it.

And there was another beast, a second one, that looked like a bear. It was raised up on one side, with three ribs between its teeth in its mouth, and these words were spoken to it: ‘Get up and eat plenty of meat!’
After this I kept looking, and there was another, like a leopard, with four bird’s wings on its back; the beast had four heads, and dominion was given to it.

After this I kept looking in the night visions, and there was a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible and exceedingly strong. It had great teeth of iron; it devoured and crushed, and what was left it trampled with its feet. It was unlike all the beasts before it, and it had ten horns.

While I was pondering the horns, another horn, a little one, came up among them, and three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots before it. In this horn were eyes like a man’s eyes and a mouth speaking great things.

“I kept watching
until thrones were placed,
and the Ancient of Days{c} sat down.
His garment was as white as snow,
and the hair of his head like clean wool;
his throne was fiery flames,
and its wheels blazing fire.

A stream of fire was pouring out
from before him.
Thousands upon thousands waited on him,
and myriads upon myriads stood in front of him.
The court took its seat,
and the books were opened.
“Then I kept watching because of the sound of the great words the horn was speaking. I watched until the beast was killed, and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire.
As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, but their lives were prolonged for a season and a time.

“In the night visions I kept watching,
and look, coming with the clouds of heaven
was someone like a son of man.{d}
He approached the Ancient of Days
and was led into his presence.

He was given authority,
glory and a kingdom,
so that every people, nation and language
would serve him.
His authority is eternal authority
that will not fade,
and his kingdom is one
that will never be destroyed.
“I, Daniel, was troubled in my spirit within me,{e} and the visions in my mind frightened me.
I went up to one of the attendants standing there and inquired of him the truth of all this. He spoke to me and let me know what these things meant:
‘These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth.
But the holy ones of the Most High{f} will receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever, forever and ever.’

“Then I wanted to learn the truth about the fourth beast, which differed from all the rest and was terrifying, with iron teeth and bronze claws, and which ate and crushed and stamped on whatever remained with its feet,
and about the ten horns on its head, and the other horn that grew up and made three fall—the horn that had eyes and a mouth that spoke boastfully, and that looked bigger than the rest.
As I looked, this horn was waging war against the holy ones and prevailing over them,
until the Ancient of Days arrived, and a verdict was given in favor of the holy ones of the Most High, and the moment came when the holy ones took over the kingdom.

“He spoke thus:
‘As for the fourth beast, there will be a fourth kingdom on earth,
unlike every other kingdom;
it will devour the whole earth,
tread it down and break it in pieces.

The ten horns:
from this kingdom ten kings will rise,
and after them yet another will rise.
He will differ from those before him,
and three kings he will humble.

Then the court will sit,
and his dominion will be removed,
to be consumed and brought to ruin forever.

Then the kingdom, the authority
and the greatness of all the kingdoms under heaven
will be given to the people who are the holy ones of the Most High.
Their kingdom is an eternal kingdom,
and every ruler will serve and obey them.’{h}
“Here the account ends. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts troubled me greatly and my face grew pale, but I kept the matter to myself.”{i}

notes.text: About 553 BC, if Belshazzar’s regency is counted from Nabonidus’s departure for Teima. Chapters 7–12 are visions told in the first person, arranged by date; chapter 7 is earlier than chapters 5–6.
In the Bible the sea often stands for the forces of chaos opposed to God (compare Isaiah 27:1; Job 26:12; Revelation 13:1).
Aramaic ʿattiq yomin, “one advanced in days,” that is, an aged one, a picture of God as eternal judge.

Aramaic kebar ʾenash, “one like a human being.” In contrast to the beasts from the sea, a humanlike figure comes with the clouds of heaven, which elsewhere in the Bible accompany God himself. In verses 18, 22, and 27 the kingdom is given to “the holy ones of the Most High,” and many interpreters take the figure as representing them; others identify him as a heavenly being, perhaps the angel Michael (compare 10:13, 21; 12:1). Later Jewish texts (1 Enoch, 4 Ezra) and the Gospels understand him as an individual, messianic figure, and Jesus uses “the Son of Man” of himself with direct reference to this verse (Mark 13:26; 14:62).
Aramaic “in the midst of its sheath,” that is, within my body.

The holy ones are probably God’s faithful people (compare verse 27, “the people of the holy ones of the Most High”), though some take them as angels. The Aramaic word for “Most High” here and in verses 22, 25, and 27 is plural in form (ʿelyonin), a plural of majesty.

That is, probably three and a half years (compare 9:27; 12:7; Revelation 12:14). Many interpreters see a reference to the persecution of the Jews by Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who in 167 BC banned the observance of the Sabbath and festivals and the keeping of the law (1 Maccabees 1:41–64).
Or “Their kingdom … serve and obey them,” referring to the people. The Aramaic pronoun is singular and can refer either to the people or to the Most High.
This is the end of the Aramaic section that began at 2:4b. From 8:1 the book is again written in Hebrew.

verses.text: In the third year of King Belshazzar’s reign, I, Daniel,{a} saw a vision, following the one I had seen earlier.
I looked in the vision, and as I looked I was at Susa the citadel, in the province of Elam; and in the vision I was by the Ulai Canal.{b}
Lifting up my eyes, I saw a ram standing before the canal. It had two horns, both of them high, but one higher than the other, and the higher one came up last.
I watched the ram charging westward, northward, and southward. No beast could stand against it, nor could anyone deliver from its hand. It did whatever it wished and grew great.
While I was thinking about this, a male goat came from the west, covering the whole earth without its feet touching the ground. Between its eyes the goat had a prominent horn.
It approached the ram with two horns that I had seen standing beside the canal, and charged at it with all its furious power.

I saw it reach the ram; it was enraged against it, struck the ram, and broke its two horns, and the ram had no strength to stand before it. It threw the ram down to the ground and trampled on it, and there was no one to rescue the ram from its power.
The male goat became enormously powerful. But when it was at its strongest, the large horn snapped off, and four prominent horns grew in its place, pointing toward the four winds of the sky.
Out of one of them came forth a single horn, a small one,{c} which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the Beautiful Land.
It grew great, even to heaven’s host, and cast down to earth some of the host and some of the stars, and trampled them.
It even made itself as great as the Prince of the host; from him the regular burnt offering{d} was taken away, and the place of his sanctuary was overthrown.
Because of transgression a host was given over to it together with the regular burnt offering,{e} and it cast truth to the ground; it acted and prospered.

Then I heard a certain holy one speak, and another holy one asked the one speaking, “How long is the vision about the regular burnt offering, and the desolating transgression,{f} and the trampling of sanctuary and host that has been permitted?”
He said to me,{g} “For two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings; then the sanctuary will be restored to its right state.”
When I, Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it; and there before me stood one who looked like a man.
And I heard a human voice between the banks of the Ulai, which called out, “Gabriel,{h} make this man understand the vision.”
He came beside the place where I was standing, and at his coming I was terrified and fell on my face. He said to me, “Understand, son of man,{i} that the vision belongs to the time of the end.”
While he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground; but he touched me and set me on my feet.
He said, “I am going to make known to you what will happen in the latter part of the wrath, for it concerns the appointed time of the end.
The two-horned ram that you saw stands for the kings of Media and Persia.
The hairy goat is the king of Greece,{j} and the large horn between its eyes is the first king.
As for the horn that was broken, in whose place four arose, four kingdoms will arise from his nation, but not with his power.
Near the end of their rule, when the rebels have done their worst, a king will appear, hard-faced{k} and skilled in trickery.
His power will be mighty, but not by his own power.{l} He will cause astounding destruction and will succeed in what he does. He will destroy mighty men and the people of the holy ones.

Through his cleverness he will make deception succeed under his control, and in his mind he will think himself great. He will destroy many people who feel secure, and he will even challenge the Prince of princes; yet he will be shattered, though not by human power.
The vision of the evenings and the mornings that was told is true. But you are to seal up the vision, for it concerns days far off.”
I, Daniel, was exhausted and was ill for several days. Afterward I got up and attended to the king’s affairs; yet I was dismayed at the vision, and no one could make it plain.{m}

notes.text: From here to the end of the book the text is in Hebrew. The Qumran manuscripts 4QDan-a and 4QDan-b, as reported, preserve this change from Aramaic back to Hebrew.
Or “the Ulai Gate.” Susa was the Persian royal winter capital (compare Nehemiah 1:1; Esther 1:2). The Ulai was a watercourse near the city.

The little horn is generally identified as Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC), of the Seleucid dynasty, one of the four kingdoms into which Alexander’s empire was divided. “The Beautiful Land” is Israel (compare 11:16, 41; Jeremiah 3:19).

Hebrew hattamid, “the continual (offering),” the burnt offering presented every morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42); likewise in verses 12–13 and at 11:31; 12:11. Antiochus stopped the temple sacrifices in December 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:45, 54).
The Hebrew of this verse is very difficult, and the translation is uncertain.
Hebrew happeshaʿ shomem. Compare “the abomination that makes desolate” at 9:27; 11:31; 12:11, and the note at 9:27.

Most Hebrew manuscripts read “to me”; the Old Greek, Theodotion, and the Syriac read “to him.” The 2,300 evenings and mornings may mean 2,300 days or, counting the evening and morning sacrifices separately, 1,150 days, roughly the period from the stopping of the sacrifices to the rededication of the temple in December 164 BC.
The name means “God is my mighty one” or “man of God.” Gabriel and Michael (10:13) are the only angels named in the Old Testament.
Hebrew ben-ʾadam, “human being,” as in Ezekiel.
Hebrew Yavan (Ionia), the usual Hebrew name for the Greeks. The first king is Alexander the Great (336–323 BC).
Hebrew “strong of face,” that is, insolent, shameless. “Skilled in intrigue” is literally “understanding riddles.”
The phrase “but not by his own power” may have been copied by mistake from verse 22.
Or “and did not understand it.”

verses.text: In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus,{a} a Mede by descent, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans—

in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of years that the word of Yahweh to the prophet Jeremiah said would have to pass before the desolation of Jerusalem ended: seventy years.{b}
Then I set my face toward the Lord God to seek him with prayer and supplications, fasting in sackcloth and ashes.
I prayed to Yahweh my God and confessed: “Lord, great and awe-inspiring God, you who keep your covenant and faithful love toward those who love you and obey your commands:
We have sinned; we have committed iniquity and done wickedly; we have rebelled and departed from your commands and your rulings.
We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land.

You, Lord, are in the right, but we are covered with shame,{c} as we are today—the people of Judah, the residents of Jerusalem, and all Israel, both nearby and far away, in every country where you scattered them because of their unfaithfulness to you.
Yahweh, open shame belongs to us, to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, because we have sinned against you.
To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, for we rebelled against him
and did not obey the voice of Yahweh our God by following the laws he gave us through his servants the prophets.

All Israel has transgressed your law and turned aside, refusing to listen to your voice. So the curse and the oath written in the law of Moses the servant of God have been poured out on us,{d} because we have sinned against him.

He has carried out his words that he spoke against us and against our rulers who ruled us,{e} by bringing on us a great calamity; for under the whole heaven nothing has been done like what has been done against Jerusalem.
Just as it stands written in the law of Moses, all this disaster has come upon us; still we have not sought the favor of Yahweh our God, turning from our iniquities and paying heed to your truth.
Therefore Yahweh kept watch over the calamity and brought it upon us, for Yahweh our God is righteous in all the works he has done, and we have not listened to his voice.
And now, Lord our God, you brought your people out of Egypt with a strong hand and made yourself famous, as you are today: but we have sinned and done evil.

Lord, in line with all your acts of justice, turn your anger and fury away from Jerusalem, your city and your holy mountain; for because of our sins and the wrongdoing of our ancestors, all our neighbors scorn Jerusalem and your people.
So now, our God, listen to your servant’s prayer and his requests for mercy, and for the sake of the Lord{f} let your face shine on your devastated sanctuary.

Incline your ear, my God, and hear; open your eyes and look upon our desolations and upon the city that bears your name. It is not on the ground of our righteous deeds that we lay our supplications before you, but on the ground of your abundant mercies.
Lord, listen! Lord, pardon! Lord, pay attention and act! Do not wait, for your own sake, my God, because your city and your people carry your name.”
While I was still speaking and praying, confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my plea before Yahweh my God on behalf of the holy mountain of my God—
yes, while I was still speaking in prayer, Gabriel—the man I had seen in the earlier vision—came close to me in swift flight{g} around the hour of the evening offering.
He gave me understanding and said to me, “Daniel, I have come out now to give you wisdom and understanding.
At the beginning of your pleas a word went out, and I have come to tell it, for you are greatly treasured.{h} So consider the word and understand the vision:

“Seventy weeks{i} have been determined for your people and your holy city:
to end rebellion,
to finish with sin,{j}
to make atonement for wrongdoing,
to bring in eternal righteousness,
to seal up vision and prophecy,
and to anoint the most holy place.{k}

Know and understand: from the going out of the word to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until an anointed one, a prince,{l} there will be seven weeks; and for sixty-two weeks it will be rebuilt, with plaza and moat, but in a time of distress.

After the sixty-two weeks an anointed one will be cut off, with nothing left to him.{m} The people of the coming prince will destroy the city and the sanctuary. The end will come like a flood, and war will continue until the end; devastations have been determined.

He will confirm a covenant with many for one week; in the middle of the week he will stop sacrifice and grain offering. On a wing of abominations will come one who devastates,{n} until the determined end is poured out on the one who devastates.”

notes.text: Hebrew ʾAḥashwerosh, the name elsewhere used of Xerxes (Esther 1:1). On Darius the Mede see the note at 5:31.
See Jeremiah 25:11–12; 29:10; compare 2 Chronicles 36:21.
Hebrew “shame of face”; likewise in verse 8.
See Leviticus 26:14–39; Deuteronomy 28:15–68.
Hebrew “our judges who judged us.”
Theodotion reads “for your sake, Lord.”
Or “when I was utterly weary”; the Hebrew is uncertain. The evening offering was made in the late afternoon (compare Exodus 29:39–41; Ezra 9:4–5).
Hebrew ḥamudot, “precious things, a treasure”; likewise at 10:11, 19.

Hebrew shavuʿim shivʿim, “seventy sevens,” that is, seventy periods of seven, generally understood as weeks of years, 490 years in all, an expansion of Jeremiah’s seventy years (verse 2; compare Leviticus 25:8; 26:18). The interpretation of verses 24–27 is among the most debated in the Bible. Many modern interpreters take the final week to be the period of the persecution under Antiochus IV (171–164 BC); traditional Christian interpretation has generally related the anointed one and the final week to Christ, and traditional Jewish interpretation to the destruction of the second temple in AD 70. The schemes differ in their starting points and in how literally they take the numbers.
So the written text (Kethiv), “to seal up sin”; the reading tradition (Qere) has “to bring sin to an end.”
Or “a most holy one.” The phrase qodesh qodashim, “holy of holies,” is used elsewhere of the sanctuary, its altar, or its holy things, never clearly of a person.

Or “the Anointed One, the Prince” or “Messiah the Prince” (so the KJV). Hebrew mashiaḥ, “anointed,” is used of kings, priests, and once of Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1); there is no article. The Masoretic punctuation separates the “seven weeks” from the “sixty-two weeks,” as here; Theodotion and the KJV join them (“seven weeks, and threescore and two weeks”). Candidates for the anointed one of this verse include Zerubbabel, the high priest Joshua, and Cyrus (compare Ezra 1:1–4; 3:2), and, on the other punctuation, Christ.

Or “and there will be no one for him.” Many see here the murder of the high priest Onias III in 171 BC (compare 11:22; 2 Maccabees 4:33–38); traditional Christian interpretation sees the death of Christ.

Hebrew shiqquṣim meshomem; compare 11:31 (“the abomination that makes desolate”) and 12:11. The phrase is probably a deliberate distortion of a title of the god Baal Shamem, “Lord of heaven,” the Syrian equivalent of Olympian Zeus, to whom Antiochus IV dedicated the Jerusalem temple and set up an altar or image on the altar of burnt offering in December 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54, “a desolating sacrilege”; 2 Maccabees 6:2). Jesus speaks of “the abomination of desolation” as a sign of the future (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14), and many Christian interpreters have referred this verse to the Roman destruction of the temple in AD 70 or to events still to come. “The wing” may mean a wing or pinnacle of the temple.

verses.text: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia{a} a word was revealed to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar. True was the word, and it concerned a great conflict.{b} He grasped the word, and understanding of the vision was given him.
In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three whole weeks.
I ate no delicacies; no meat or wine entered my mouth, and I did not anoint myself at all until the three weeks were over.
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month (in March–April),{c} as I was on the bank of the great river, the Tigris,{d}
I raised my eyes and looked, and behold, a man dressed in linen, his waist girded with gold of Uphaz.{e}

His body was like chrysolite,{f} his face had the appearance of lightning, his eyes were like torches of fire, his arms and feet gleamed like polished bronze, and his words sounded like the noise of a crowd.
I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; the men who were with me did not see it, but a great trembling fell on them, and they fled to hide themselves.
So I was left alone and saw this great vision. No strength remained in me; my vigor was turned to pallor,{g} and I kept no strength.
Yet I heard the sound of his words; and on hearing them I sank into a deep sleep upon my face, my face toward the ground.
Then a hand touched me and set me trembling on my knees and the palms of my hands.

He said to me, “Daniel, you are highly esteemed; understand the words I am about to tell you, and stand up straight, because I have now been sent to you.” When he had said this, I rose to my feet, shaking.
He said to me, “Do not fear, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I have come because of your words.
The prince of the kingdom of Persia{h} withstood me twenty-one days, but Michael,{i} one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I left him there with the kings of Persia.{j}
I have come to make you understand what will happen to your people in the latter days, for there is yet a vision for those days.”
While he was speaking these words with me, I turned my face toward the ground and was speechless.

Then one in the likeness of the sons of men touched my lips, and I opened my mouth and spoke. I said to the one standing before me, “My lord, because of the vision pains have come upon me,{k} and I have kept no strength.
How can my lord’s servant, such as I am, talk with my lord? As for me, no strength remains in me now, and no breath is left in me.”
Again one who looked like a man touched me, and he gave me strength.
He said, “Do not fear, man greatly treasured. Peace be with you; be strong, be strong!” As he spoke with me I was strengthened, and I said, “Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me.”
Then he said, “Do you know why I have come to you? Now I will return to fight against the prince of Persia; and when I go out, behold, the prince of Greece will come.
Yet I will declare to you what is written in the book of truth. Not one stands firm beside me against these but Michael, your prince.

notes.text: That is, 536 BC.
Or “and of great hardship”; Hebrew tsavaʾ gadol, “a great host” or “a hard service.”
Hebrew “the first month,” Nisan. The fast of verses 2–3 would have included Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread (the 14th to the 21st of the month).
Hebrew Ḥiddeqel. The Syriac reads “the Euphrates,” which is usually called “the great river” (Genesis 15:18).
An unknown place; perhaps a corruption of Ophir (compare Jeremiah 10:9).
Hebrew tarshish, a precious stone of uncertain identity, perhaps yellow jasper or topaz.
Hebrew “my splendor was changed upon me to ruin.”

A heavenly being who represents and champions Persia, as Michael does Israel (verse 21; 12:1); compare Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Septuagint and Qumran readings (“according to the number of the sons of God”).
The name means “Who is like God?”
So the Hebrew; the Old Greek and Theodotion read “I left him there with the prince of the kingdom of Persia.”
Hebrew “my pangs are turned upon me,” the word used of a woman’s labor pains.

verses.text: “And as for me, in the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him.{a}

Now I will declare the truth to you. Three more kings will arise in Persia, and a fourth will be far richer than all of them. When he has grown strong through his riches, he will stir up everyone against the kingdom of Greece.{b}
Then a warrior king will stand up and hold sway over a vast dominion, doing whatever he wishes.{c}

But as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom will be broken and parceled out toward the four winds of heaven, but not to his descendants, nor with the dominion that he wielded; for his kingdom will be uprooted and go to others besides these.
“Then the king of the south will grow strong, but one of his commanders will grow stronger than he and will rule a dominion greater than his.{d}

Some years later they will make a pact: the daughter of the king of the south will go to the king of the north to establish an agreement. But she will not keep her power, and neither he nor his power will last; she will be handed over, along with her escorts, her child{e} and the one who backed her in those days.
But a branch from her family line will rise to take his place.{f} He will attack the army and enter the stronghold of the king of the north, and he will fight them and win.

He will even seize their gods, along with their cast idols and their valuable articles of silver and gold, and take them off as plunder to Egypt; and for some years he will stay away from the king of the north.
Then the king of the north will attack the kingdom of the king of the south, but will return to his own country.
“His sons will wage war and gather a multitude of great forces, which will keep coming on and overflow like a flood and pass through, and again carry the war as far as his fortress.{g}
Then the king of the south, moved with rage, will go out and fight against him, the king of the north, who will raise a great multitude; but the multitude will be given into the hand of his enemy.{h}
When the multitude is carried off, his heart will be exalted; he will bring down tens of thousands, but he will not prevail.
For the king of the north will raise another army, larger than the first, and after some years{i} he will march out with a huge force and plenty of equipment.
In those times many will rise up against the king of the south, and the violent men among your own people will lift themselves up to fulfill the vision, but they will stumble.

Then the king of the north will come and throw up siege mounds and capture a well-fortified city. The forces of the south will not stand, nor even his choice troops; there will be no strength to stand.{j}
But he who comes against him will do as he wills, and no one will stand before him. He will take his stand in the Beautiful Land, with destruction in his hand.

He will set his face to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and he will make an agreement with him and give him a daughter in marriage{k} to destroy the kingdom;{l} but it will not stand or serve his purpose.
After that he will turn his attention to the coastlands and take many of them. But a commander will stop his insolence; yes, he will repay him for his insolence.{m}
Then he will turn his face back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he will stumble and fall and be found no more.
Then there will arise in his place one who will send out an exactor of tribute through the glory of the kingdom;{n} but within a few days he will be broken, neither in anger nor in battle.
“A despicable person{o} will take his place, someone who was never given the honor of royalty. He will arrive when no one expects it and take over the kingdom through trickery.
Armies will be utterly swept away before him like a flood and broken, and the prince of the covenant{p} as well.
From the time an alliance is made with him he will practice deceit; he will go up and become strong with only a few people.

Stealthily he will invade the richest places of the province and do what none of his fathers or his fathers’ fathers ever did, distributing among them plunder, spoil, and goods. Against fortresses he will devise his schemes, but only for a time.

He will stir up his power and his heart against the king of the south with a great army. The king of the south will wage war with an exceedingly great and mighty army, but he will not stand, for they will devise plans against him.{q}
Those who eat his rich food will break him; his army will be swept away, and many will fall slain.
As for the two kings, their hearts will be set on evil; at one table they will speak lies. But it will not succeed, for the end is yet to be at the appointed time.
Then he will go back to his land laden with riches, his heart opposed to the holy covenant. He will work his will and return to his own land.{r}
“At the appointed time he will come back into the south, but this time it will not be as it was before.

Ships from Kittim{s} will oppose him, and he will lose courage and turn back. He will be furious at the holy covenant and act against it; he will return and show favor to those who abandon the holy covenant.
His armed forces will rise up and defile the sanctuary fortress. They will remove the daily burnt offering and set up the abomination that causes devastation.{t}
Those who act wickedly against the covenant he will corrupt with smooth words, but the people who know their God will stand firm and take action.
The wise among the people{u} will give understanding to many, though for some days they will fall by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder.
As they fall, a little help will come to them,{v} and many will attach themselves to them with flattery.
Some of the wise will fall, so that refining, purifying, and cleansing may be done among them until the time of the end, for it is still to come at the appointed time.

“The king will do whatever he pleases. He will lift himself up and make himself greater than any god, and he will say astonishing things against the God of gods. He will do well until the time of wrath ends, because what has been decided will take place.
He will ignore the gods of his ancestors and the one women desire,{w} and he will ignore every other god, because he will make himself greater than all of them.
Instead, he will honor the god of fortresses—a god his fathers did not know he will honor with gold and silver, with precious stones and costly things.{x}

He will attack the most heavily defended strongholds with the aid of a foreign god. He will shower honor on those who recognize him, put them in authority over many, and distribute land in return for payment.

“At the time of the end the king of the south will clash with him, and the king of the north will storm against him with chariots and horsemen and many ships. He will enter countries and overflow and pass through.{y}
He will enter the Beautiful Land, and many{z} will stumble; but these will be rescued from his hand: Edom, Moab, and the chief part of the Ammonites.
He will stretch out his hand against countries, and the land of Egypt will not escape.
He will gain control of the treasures of gold and silver and of all the precious things of Egypt, and the Libyans and Cushites{aa} will follow in his train.
But news from the east and the north will terrify him, and in a great rage he will set out to destroy and to devote many to destruction.
He will pitch his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain. Yet his end will come, and no one will help him.

notes.text: The Hebrew is abrupt; “him” is probably Michael (10:21). The Old Greek and Theodotion read “in the first year of Cyrus.” Chapter 11 surveys, in the form of prophecy and without naming names, the history of the Persian kings, Alexander the Great, and the wars between the Ptolemies of Egypt (“the king of the south”) and the Seleucids of Syria (“the king of the north”), culminating in Antiochus IV Epiphanes (verses 21–45). The identifications given in these notes are those commonly proposed.
The fourth king is probably Xerxes I (486–465 BC), who invaded Greece in 480 BC.
Alexander the Great.
Ptolemy I of Egypt and his former general Seleucus I, founder of the Seleucid kingdom.

So the ancient versions; the Hebrew reads “the one who fathered her.” Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, married Antiochus II (about 252 BC); she, her son, and her attendants were murdered after his death.
Ptolemy III, Berenice’s brother, who invaded the Seleucid kingdom in 246 BC.
The sons of Seleucus II: Seleucus III and Antiochus III “the Great.”
The battle of Raphia (217 BC), where Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III.
Hebrew “at the end of the times, years.”
Probably the capture of Sidon by Antiochus III in about 199 BC.
Hebrew “the daughter of women.” Antiochus III gave his daughter Cleopatra I in marriage to Ptolemy V in 194/193 BC.
Or “to destroy him”; the Hebrew is literally “to destroy her.”
The Roman consul Lucius Scipio defeated Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC. The Hebrew of the last clause is difficult.
Seleucus IV (187–175 BC), whose minister Heliodorus tried to seize the temple treasury (2 Maccabees 3); “the glory of the kingdom” is probably Jerusalem or its temple.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC), who took the throne in place of the legitimate heir, his nephew Demetrius.
Probably the high priest Onias III, deposed in 175 BC and murdered in 171 BC (compare 9:26).
Antiochus IV’s first invasion of Egypt (170–169 BC) against Ptolemy VI.
In 169 BC Antiochus plundered the temple in Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 1:20–24).
Kittim originally meant Cyprus, then the western lands generally; here the Romans, whose envoy Popillius Laenas forced Antiochus to leave Egypt in 168 BC. The Old Greek reads “Romans.”
Hebrew hashshiqquṣ meshomem. See the note at 9:27, and compare 8:13; 12:11; 1 Maccabees 1:54; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14.
Hebrew maskilim, “those who have insight” or “who make others wise”; likewise in verse 35 and at 12:3, 10.
Often taken as a reference to the Maccabean revolt, which began in 167 BC.
Probably the god Tammuz-Adonis (compare Ezekiel 8:14).
Probably Olympian Zeus, whose cult Antiochus promoted, or Jupiter Capitolinus of Rome.

Verses 40–45 do not correspond to any known events of Antiochus’s last years; he died in Persia in 164 BC, not between the sea and Jerusalem (verse 45). Many scholars therefore think that the author’s historical survey ends at verse 39 and that what follows is genuine prediction; others apply these verses to a figure of the last days.
Or, with a slight change of vowels, “tens of thousands.”
That is, the people of the upper Nile region (ancient Nubia).

verses.text:
“At that time Michael will arise,
the great prince who stands guard over your people.
There will be a time of distress
such as has not been since there was a nation
until that time.
But at that time your people will be delivered,
everyone who is found written in the book.

The wise will be radiant
like the shining of the firmament,{b}
and those who bring many to righteousness
will be as the stars, forever and ever.
But you, Daniel, keep the words secret and seal the book until the time of the end. Many will run to and fro, and knowledge will increase.”{c}
Then I, Daniel, looked, and two more figures were standing there, one on this side of the river and the other on the opposite side.
One of them asked the man dressed in linen, who was above the water of the river, “How long will it be before these amazing events end?”

I heard the man dressed in linen, who was above the water of the river, raise both his right and left hands to heaven and swear by the one who lives forever that it would be a time, times and half a time;{d} and when the breaking of the holy people’s power is complete, all these things will be finished.
I heard, but I did not understand. So I said, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?”
He said, “Go your way, Daniel, for the words are kept secret and sealed until the time of the end.
Many will purify themselves, make themselves white, and be refined, but the wicked will act wickedly. None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand.
From the time the daily burnt offering is stopped and the abomination that causes devastation{e} is set up, there will be 1,290 days.
Blessed is the one who waits and reaches 1,335 days.
But you, go your way until the end. You will rest, and you will rise to your allotted place at the end of the days.”{f}

notes.text: This is the clearest statement in the Old Testament of a resurrection of the dead to judgment (compare Isaiah 26:19). Hebrew deraʾon, “contempt, abhorrence,” occurs elsewhere only in Isaiah 66:24.
Hebrew raqiaʿ, the “expanse” or “firmament” of Genesis 1:6–8.
The Old Greek reads “until many go mad and the earth is filled with wrongdoing.”
See the note at 7:25.

See the notes at 9:27 and 11:31. The figures of 1,290 days here and 1,335 days in verse 12 both slightly exceed three and a half years (compare 7:25; 8:14); they may be successive recalculations of the expected end.

Here the Hebrew-Aramaic book of Daniel ends. The Greek versions add the stories of Susanna (placed before chapter 1 in Theodotion) and of Bel and the Dragon (after chapter 12); see the note at 3:23 and the source note.
